summary:
The Problem: When Noise Masquerades as Trend
Detecting genuine environmental trends is difficult due to seasonal cycles, extreme weather, sensor drift, and autocorrelation. Traditional statistical tests can mistake natural variations for long-term climate changes, producing false alarms.

The Solution: TrendScope
TrendScope is a climate analysis platform using NASA POWER monthly data (MERRA-2 and CERES) from 2001–2024. It applies four statistical methods:

Seasonal Adjustment: Removes recurring monthly patterns.
Yue-Pilon TFPW: Corrects autocorrelation while preserving genuine trends.
Theil-Sen Estimator: Calculates robust trends with 95% confidence intervals.
Benjamini-Hochberg FDR: Controls false discoveries across spatial grids.

The statistical engine achieves 100% numerical parity with pymannkendall 1.4.3.

Key Features & Discoveries
Planetary Radar: Analyses five climate variables across Svalbard, Manaus, Chennai, and Jaipur.
Indian Grid Analysis: Examines 16 spatial cells, finding 11 significant warming cells (up to +0.31°C/decade) and five neutral or cooling cells (down to -0.29°C/decade).
No-Trend Detection: Shows Chennai's temperature trend is insignificant (p=0.2755) after autocorrelation correction.
Time-to-Significance: Estimates the observation period needed to detect genuine trends
Open Science: Supports NASA data analysis, CSV/PNG exports, shareable links, and offline access.

TrendScope makes climate trend detection more reliable, transparent, and accessible.
details:
GITHUB LINK: https://github.com/harishcjcoder/TrendScope
What it does and how it works
TrendScope is a free web tool that helps students and the public find out whether a change in Earth’s climate is real or just random variation. The user picks a NASA variable (air temperature, rainfall, humidity, root-zone soil wetness, or surface sunlight) and a location by typing coordinates or choosing a preset. The tool fetches 24 years (2001–2024) of monthly NASA POWER data, removes the seasonal cycle, and draws the time series with a trend line and 95% confidence band. It then answers four questions: What is changing? Where? How much (per decade)? Is it statistically significant? The trend is estimated with the Theil-Sen slope and tested with Mann-Kendall, using trend-free pre-whitening to correct for autocorrelation. We show both the naive and corrected p-values. A Trend Radar ranks the variables for a place. A 4×4 Trend Map of India shows where a variable rises or falls, with false-discovery-rate (Benjamini-Hochberg) correction. Case Files give four ready examples, and a Reliability score and a time-to-significance estimate show how much to trust a result.

Benefits
Users don’t need statistics knowledge. Results come with plain-language explanations, definitions, and honest “not significant” verdicts. The interface offers Simple and Scientist modes, English, Tamil and Hindi, dark mode, and CSV, PNG and share-link exports.

Intended impact
We want to build data literacy and show that trends must be tested before they are believed. This makes NASA Earth data easier to use in classrooms and for anyone curious about their local climate.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the front end and the statistics engine; Node.js scripts to build cached case data; a Netlify serverless function as a fallback proxy; Netlify for hosting. Data comes from the NASA POWER API (MERRA-2 and CERES-based products). We validated our statistics against Python’s pymannkendall. [Add any AI coding or design tools your team used.]

Creativity
We combine the “detective” idea with scientific rigour. The tool corrects for autocorrelation, controls false discoveries across the map, flags short or weak records, and estimates how much longer a record would need to become significant. It can also show opposite trends within the same region, which the challenge highlights.

Factors we considered
Accuracy, since we validated the engine and excluded fill values. Honesty about uncertainty and the fact that correlation is not causation. Reliability, since cached examples work if the API is slow. Accessibility, with colour-blind-safe colours, keyboard use, and multiple languages. Limits: monthly resolution, linear trends only, and model-derived data.
